Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/AFP/Getty Images India Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs Penelope MacRae in Delhi Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature. Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd. The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement , a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister. Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released. “The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India. How gen Z exposed India’s prime-time propaganda machine Read more The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations. They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance. Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits. Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies. View image in fullscreen Police use water cannon to disperse demonstrators during a protest. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar/AFP/Getty Images The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is India Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India after newsletter promotion The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said. The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned. The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35. Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed. Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPA Indonesia Rescue teams search for survivors in Indonesia after powerful earthquake Searchers dig through collapsed buildings and debris after 7.7 magnitude quake killed at least 47 people Associated Press Sat 15 Aug 2026 23.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rescue crews dug through collapsed buildings and landslide debris in eastern Indonesia on Sunday as they searched for bodies and possible survivors a day after a powerful earthquake killed at least 47 people, injured more than 100 and displaced thousands. At least 24 people died in Manggarai regency and 17 in neighbouring East Manggarai, with additional fatalities reported in Sikka, Ngada and Ende regencies, the national disaster management agency said. Rescuers were still searching for people feared buried beneath landslides triggered by the quake across six regencies on Flores, a predominantly Catholic island in Muslim-majority Indonesia . Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern Indonesia Read more The magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck 68km (42 miles) north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province, the USGS said. The quake, at a depth of about 10km (6 miles) off the coast of Flores, rattled much of the island and sent residents fleeing in panic. Tremors were also felt in neighbouring West Nusa Tenggara and parts of southern Sulawesi. View image in fullscreen A crack in the road in East Nusa Tenggara after the quake. Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPA The disaster agency said the quake destroyed more than 900 homes and damaged nearly 450 more, forcing about 5,000 people into temporary shelters. Thousands more spent the night outdoors, fearing strong aftershocks. At least 167 public facilities, including schools, health centres and churches, were also damaged. Relief workers have begun distributing rice, ready-to-eat meals, drinking water, blankets and medicine, while emergency shelters were being set up for displaced residents. Authorities said restoring electricity and communications as well as delivering aid to remote villages isolated by landslides remained among the biggest challenges. View image in fullscreen Earthquake victims are treated in a temporary medical tent amid fears of aftershocks in Ruteng. Photograph: Juni Kriswanto/AFP/Getty Images The quake also struck Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo national park, one of Indonesia’s best-known tourist destinations. Landslides blocked sections of the Trans-Flores Highway, a roughly 700km (435 mile) road linking communities across the mountainous island. Many residents continued to sleep outside rather than risk returning to damaged homes. “The shaking was terrifying, so intense that my house nearly collapsed,” said Anastasia Imad, a farmer in Labuan Bajo, speaking from a makeshift green tent beside her damaged home. “We feared the aftershocks would bring it down on us while we slept.” View image in fullscreen People in the coastal village of Nangahale in Sikka regency spent the night in a field. Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/Getty Images Teams resumed searches on Sunday in areas that had remained inaccessible since the quake, particularly in Manggarai, East Manggarai and Nagekeo regencies. “We have cleared most landslides and reopened roads to previously isolated villages, although communication disruptions and power outages continue to hamper search efforts,” said Fathur Rahman, head of the search and rescue office in Maumere, the capital of Sikka regency. He said rescuers were focusing on searching the rubble of collapsed homes and other buildings for possible victims. Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions because of its location on the Pacific “ring of fire”, a horseshoe-shaped arc of seismic faults and volcanoes. Flores has experienced some of the country’s deadliest disasters. A powerful earthquake and tsunami in 1992 killed about 2,500 people on the island. In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake triggered a tsunami on Sulawesi that killed more than 4,400 people. In 2004, a magnitude 9.1 quake off Sumatra unleashed a tsunami that killed about 230,000 people in a dozen countries. https://www.politico.eu/article/ai-is-he.text: Criminal gangs are using artificial intelligence to help them find locations in Europe to build illicit cigarette factories with less chance of getting caught, an EU auditor warned on Tuesday. These gangs used to operate in Eastern Europe where it was easier to hide, Petri Sarvamaa in charge of the European Court of Auditor’s report on illicit tobacco , told a press briefing. Now, with AI, it’s easier to find places to operate that are closer to their markets, he said, in rural locations and villages. “This reduces the risk in the supply chain for the criminals,” added Esther Torrente Heras, senior auditor. Advertisement Advertisement It’s just one of the many challenges facing EU and member countries as they grapple to clamp down on illicit tobacco networks, which cause at least €13 billion in lost revenue in the bloc annually. In 2023, almost one in 10 cigarettes in Europe was illegally produced or smuggled in. The report also lands as EU countries' attempts to find agreement on raising minimum tobacco and vape taxation levels have slowed after snus-loving Sweden — which is holding a general election next week — rebuffed a levy on nicotine pouches. The aim of the law is to harmonize prices across the bloc, strengthening the single market while nudging smokers to quit. A lack of coordination and intelligence sharing between EU agencies and member countries’ authorities is hindering the bloc’s response to new cigarette factories, meaning “most alarmingly” the true size, structure and economic impact is unknown, Sarvamaa said. To clamp down on this illegal activity, “it all starts with the Commission,” Sarvamaa said. “Better intelligence sharing between all relevant actors is essential.” And the Commission needs to take a greater role in coordinating a strategic response of these actors, he added, including: the European Anti-Fraud Oﬃce OLAF, Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor's Oﬃce, EPPO. The Commission broadly accepted ECA’s recommendations, bar areas it said were beyond its role. It pushed back on defining strategies for the various EU authorities, noting that OLAF and others are responsible for setting their own strategic priorities. And it said it was not possible to provide a robust approach to assessing the size and economic impact of illicit trade, since no single method could do this. “The union cannot afford to lose this fight,” Sarvamaa warned, saying that public health, safeguarding the integrity of the single market and preventing organized crime were all at risk. But he stopped short of recommending how Europe should proceed with its overhaul of tobacco products and excise legislation, saying this was a role for policy and lawmakers. Painted on a wall in the Polish city of Rzeszów, the graffiti was reportedly created as a... pic.twitter.com/FP1HYP0cDZ — Remix News & Views (@RMXnews) August 25, 2026 Polish police have reportedly secured surveillance footage and referred the case to Polish prosecutors. However, Polish newspaper toRzeszow claims that cameras are not in the direct area where the wall was painted, making it difficult to identify the suspects. Authorities also painted over the entire wall. Major Polish news outlet wPolsce24 has reacted with outrage to the investigation: "The Rzeszów case is part of a broader trend of suppressing the voices of white people who dare to remind them that their lives also have value. When black people say "Black Lives Matter," it is a fight for equality. When white people say "White Lives Matter," it is immediately racist. " The news outlet further writes: "The slogan on the garages in Rzeszów was not an expression of hatred. There was a voice reminding us that white lives matters too. And as long as we treat some lives as 'more equal' than others, such slogans will appear on walls." Meanwhile, authorities claim the graffiti is illegal under article 257 of the Polish penal code, which concerns the public insult of a group of people or an individual based on national, ethnic, or racial identity. A group labeled "Narodowy Rzeszów" allegedly posted a video of themselves standing next to the graffiti holding a banner and flares and displaying the logo of the right-wing National-Radical Camp (ONR), however, it remains unclear if they sprayed the graffiti themselves.
